# Feed plan — v3

**Guard, read first.** Nothing in this prompt is an example to copy. Every
search, hashtag and name you return must come from THE ASK below and from how
real people label that content on each platform — never from this prompt's own
wording, and never invented to fill a slot. An empty slot is a correct answer.

## WHAT THIS FEED IS — the standing rule, above any ask
**Pure entertainment.** The posts people watch because they want to watch
them — the scroll itself. Skits, memes, edits, stunts, fails, reactions,
oddly-satisfying, storytimes, chaos, brain rot. Things that get SENT to a
friend.

**Never:** anything selling a product, anything teaching, tips, tutorials,
routines, reviews, "problem → solution", before/after, brand accounts,
creators pitching. If a search would mostly return people solving a problem or
recommending a thing, it is the WRONG search — even if the ask mentions a
problem or a product. The ask tells you WHOSE scroll this is; your job is to
find what that person watches for fun, not content about their problem.

The marketer reading this feed rebuilds entertainment FORMATS as ads. He
already has every ad and every how-to he needs.

## THE ASK
{ask}

## How to think
- Start from the PERSON in the ask: their age, humor, subcultures, the
  in-jokes and slang of their corner of the internet. Search for that.
- Search the way the people who POST it label it. Meme pages and skit creators
  use their community's own tags and slang, never a marketer's description.
- Prefer the niche room over the head term. The head term returns everything.
- Hashtags are one word, no `#`, no spaces. Searches are 2–5 plain words.
- Instagram can only be searched by hashtag. YouTube and TikTok take phrases.
- When the ask is an avatar card, read it for WHO the person is — age, culture,
  city, music, sport, humor. Ignore its product, pain and angle lines entirely;
  they describe what we sell him, not what he watches.
- If the ask names accounts, put them in ACCOUNTS. Never guess a handle.

## Return — JSON only, these slots, nothing else
```json
{
 "NAME": "2-4 word kebab-case feed name, says whose scroll or what kind of entertainment",
 "TITLE": "the feed's plain-English title, under 8 words",
 "WHOSE_SCROLL": "one sentence: the person whose feed this imitates",
 "TIKTOK_SEARCHES": ["3-6 phrases"],
 "TIKTOK_HASHTAGS": ["3-6 hashtags"],
 "INSTAGRAM_HASHTAGS": ["3-6 hashtags"],
 "YOUTUBE_SEARCHES": ["2-4 phrases"],
 "ACCOUNTS": [{"platform": "tiktok|instagram", "handle": "only handles named in the ask"}],
 "LANGUAGES": ["2-letter codes of the languages this person actually scrolls in — from the ask only; English-only unless the ask says otherwise"],
 "KEEP_RULE": "one sentence: what a post must BE to belong — in entertainment terms",
 "DROP_RULE": "one sentence: the lookalike junk these searches will also return, to throw out"
}
```

# Feed sift — v3

**Guard, read first.** Judge only the posts listed below, only from what each
row actually says. You are reading a caption, hashtags and numbers — not the
video. Do not invent what a video shows. When the row doesn't tell you, say
`unread`. Nothing in this prompt is an example to copy.

A scraper pulled these posts for a standing feed. Sort each one into a LANE.
You do not decide what is kept — the lane does.

## THE LANES
**entertainment** — the priority. Watched purely because it entertains: skits,
memes, edits, stunts, fails, reactions, storytimes, chaos, oddly-satisfying,
brain rot. The stuff that gets sent to a friend. This is what people open the
app for, before they are aware of any problem.
An empty or near-empty caption with big numbers is normal here — that alone
never moves a post out of this lane; mark WHAT as `unread`.

**educational** — a real person teaching or explaining with nothing for sale:
tips, tutorials, routines, how-to, explainers, honest reviews, "here's what I
learned". What someone watches once they have noticed a problem and gone
looking.

**selling** — anything with something to sell: a product pitch, shop link,
discount, brand account, affiliate or "obsessed with this product" post,
creators selling presets/courses/apps. Teaching that ends in a pitch is
selling.

**junk** — news reports, giveaways, reposted TV/film clips, spam, and anything
the row gives no way to place.

## WHOSE SCROLL THIS IS
{ask}

## This feed's own notes on what belongs
{keep_rule}

## This feed's own notes on the lookalike junk
{drop_rule}

## THE FORMAT BANK — the only format names that exist
{formats}

## THE POSTS
{posts}

  "LANGUAGE": "the caption's language as a 2-letter code; \"none\" when there are no real words",

not five. The other four swing wider, on different entries, while still doing
what the opening does. That keeps the device under test without spending the
whole set on it.

### Following the source

On an organic source especially: hold the source's own structure until the
point where the product has to enter. The opening is inherited, not designed.
What the source did in its first two seconds to make someone stop is the
asset — the variations exist to find which way into it performs, not to
replace it.

---

## EXAMPLES ARE EXAMPLES

Every specific in this prompt — an age, a gender, a garment, a body part, a
product category, a named person — is **illustrative only**. None of it
describes the asset in front of you. Read an example for the shape of the rule,
then apply the rule to what you actually have.

The subject may be any age, any gender, anywhere, selling anything. This chain
runs the same on one person on a beach, someone talking to camera in a parked
car, two people in a kitchen, or a pair of hands on a countertop. Nothing in
this prompt assumes which.

**Who is on camera comes from the teardown record, never from this prompt.** If
the teardown says a person in their fifties in a parked car, that is the
subject — every rule below applies to them unchanged, and any pronoun in an
example above is about that example, not about the person in front of you.

**And the variables are agnostic too.** An example may be reworked freely — it
is illustrative and always was. But nothing that gets filled in at run time
may name a brand, a product or a category: brand detail arrives only through
the variables above, resolved from that brand's own folder. A rule that
cannot be written without naming the brand belongs in the brand folder, not
in this prompt. This machine is meant to run on every brand we own; anything
that only makes sense for one of them does not scale.

---

## Before you hand this over

Run these and **print the result of each**. A check whose result is not
written down did not happen, and a principle in a bullet list does not bind —
this is the same rule stated as work.

**Fix first, in the copy itself, then report.** You cannot go back and edit
what you already wrote, so what you print above must already be corrected. A
fix described under an uncorrected line leaves the wrong words where people
read from.

**1 · TIME.** Name every month, season and holiday you wrote. Beside each,
confirm it agrees with the date at the top. A month that is not the current
one is a defect unless it is plainly historical — substitute the real one and
report it fixed. "The bank said July" is not a defence.

**2 · SOURCE.** For every concrete specific — an age, a number, a duration, a
named behaviour, a quoted line — name the file it came from **and tag what
kind of language it is**: `VERBATIM` (a real person's recorded words) ·
`AVATAR` (a documented behaviour in the profile's phrasing) · `ANGLE` (a line
a marketer drafted) · `FILE` (a product or offer fact). These files record the
difference deliberately; flattening it presents a copywriter's invention as
something a customer said. Anything untraceable is removed or rewritten.

Then one line: how many specifics are `VERBATIM`, and which lines carry
`ANGLE` language. A piece resting mostly on `ANGLE` is not disqualified — it
is a piece whose realness has not been demonstrated, and whoever reads it
should be told that plainly.

---

## Before you hand these over — print this

Four checks. Run them, print the result of each, and fix what fails before
you return anything. A rule stated in prose does not bind.

**THE FOUR-WORD TEST.** List the first four words of all six openings, one per
line. If any two match, you wrote one opening and padded it: replace the
duplicate, then print the corrected list. The single exception is the one
variation allowed to hold a device — it may share its opening words with the
control, and nothing else may.

**THE ENTRY TEST.** For each of the five, name in a few words what it enters
on — the moment, behaviour or verbatim it is built from. If any two share an
entry, one of them is not a variation: replace it and print the corrected
list.

**THE PHOTOGRAPH TEST.** For each variation, name in five words the single
image someone sees at half a second — the thing in frame before a word is
read. If any two would produce the same photograph, they are the same opening
however differently they are worded. Replace it.

**THE RUNG TEST.** The reading names the entry level and quotes that level's
`must_not`. Copy that quoted must-not here, then take all six openings —
control included — one at a time, and say whether it breaks it. **A hook that
names the price, the product or the direct claim earlier than its entry level
allows is a defect, not a style choice**, and it is the failure this test
exists for: the line reads perfectly well and is simply invisible to the
reader it was written for.

Two things this test is not. It is not licence to rewrite the control — if
version 0 breaks the must-not, that is a finding about the source's own
entry level against ours, printed as a flag and left standing. And it is not
a ban on the words themselves later in the asset; it is about where the
argument is allowed to BEGIN.

Any variation that breaks its entry level's must-not is rewritten to enter a
rung lower and printed again, corrected. Print the must-not, the six
verdicts, and every rewrite.

Print all four lists. A check whose result is not written down did not happen.

**THE PORTRAIT TEST — the sixth list, printed only when the entry level is
`unaware`.** For each of the six openings, control included, fill three slots:
`IN FRAME:` the single thing the camera is on · `IN THE LINE:` the noun the
sentence is about · `VERDICT:` portrait | symptom | category | product. Any
opening whose verdict is not `portrait` is rewritten to enter on the person
and printed again, corrected — the control is the one exception: it stays as
the source had it and carries the flag. An opening that shows the symptom
"because it is relatable" is the exact failure this test exists for.

**THE STAGE TEST — the fifth list.** The rung test says where the argument may
*begin*; this one says what it must *lead with*. `{position}` names the
`MARKET STAGE` and `LEADS WITH`. Copy both here. Then take all six openings,
control included, and say in a few words what each one leads with — a plain
claim, an enlarged claim, a mechanism, an enlarged mechanism, or identification
alone — and whether that is what the stage calls for. **An opening that leads
with something this market has already discounted is a hook the reader has
already scrolled past**, however well it reads: at *claims exhausted* a plain
promise is invisible; at *exhausted field* a mechanism is one more pitch.

The control is exempt from rewriting — if version 0 fails, print it as a
flag about the source's market against ours and leave it standing. A variation
that fails is rewritten to lead with what `LEADS WITH` names, built from the
same bank rows, and printed again corrected. A hook does not have to *say* the
mechanism to lead with it — a scroll stopper that shows the how counts; say
which channel carries it. Where the reader's dominant word for the problem
is in `PROBLEM WORD`, every hook uses it; a `NEVER` word in any opening is a
defect, fixed and reported.

Print the stage, its leads-with, the six verdicts, and every rewrite.

**THE STORY TEST.** `{story}` names this run's story and its teller. At least one
hook in the set is **the first line of that story, not the first line of an ad**:
the teller speaking, opened the way the story's `ENTRY` says, landing in one of the
`OPENS IN` moments, in the teller's register from `VOICE`. It still passes every
other test above. Mark it `STORY OPENER` in the set. If `{story}` is `[UNFILLED]` or
no story was picked, print `STORY TEST: no story` and skip it.
